stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate.numerator: nodes where all 3 models returned grounded==true AND the LLM judge found semantic agreement
stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run
stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate.basis: does NOT require citation verification or a clean adversarial check -- purely: did the 3 models derive the same rule from the cited text, independently.

citation_verification_rate.numerator: nodes where every cited source's quoted_text verified as a substring of the fetched page
citation_verification_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run (null/not computed if --skip-citation-check)
citation_verification_rate.basis: mechanical HTTP fetch + substring match, no model involved.

stage_b_parse_success_rate.numerator: nodes where the adversarial call returned parseable edge_cases (not truncated, not empty, no error) -- even after the round-23/24 retry
stage_b_parse_success_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run
stage_b_parse_success_rate.basis: an infrastructure/reliability signal, not a gap-count -- a node can parse successfully and still expose real gaps, or fail to parse and expose none we know of.

full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate.stage: all three stages combined -- this is the renamed former 'grounded_agreement_rate' (round 26; the old name was found to be mislabeled relative to its own definition, see docs/DEBT_PROJECT_ARCHITECTURE_SPEC.md S4's round-24 entry)
full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate.denominator: all demo-corpus nodes attempted this run
full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate.basis: CLEAN-PASS = LLM-judged semantic agreement across all 3 grounded derivations AND all citations live-verified AND no adversarial gap found AND the adversarial check itself parsed successfully (round 26 -- a Stage B parse failure no longer silently reads as "no gaps", see spec S4). Numeric fingerprint is a secondary diagnostic only as of 2026-08-26 round 3, not part of this basis either.

grounded_agreement_rate.note: Deprecated alias for full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate (round 26), kept only so anything still reading this exact key doesn't break. This name was found to be mislabeled -- it was never actually a Stage-A-only measure despite the name. Use full_pipeline_clean_pass_rate (the honest name for the same number) or stage_a_grounded_agreement_rate (genuinely Stage-A-only) going forward.

scenario_pass_rate.stage: scenario level (depends on multiple nodes' CLEAN-PASS status)
scenario_pass_rate.numerator: concept-demo scenarios where every node_id they depend on is CLEAN-PASS this run
scenario_pass_rate.denominator: all concept-demo scenarios defined in the scenarios file
scenario_pass_rate.basis: a scenario passes iff every node_id it depends on is CLEAN-PASS in this same run

results.derivation_summary: Under 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)(i), a debt collector is presumed to comply with the harassment prohibition in § 1006.14(b)(1) and FDCPA § 806(5) if, as to a particular person and a particular debt, it places no more than seven calls within seven consecutive days and does not call within seven consecutive days after having had a telephone conversation with that person about that debt (the conversation date counts as day one). Conversely, under (b)(2)(ii), exceeding either of those frequencies creates a presumption of violation. Both presumptions are subject to the exclusions in paragraph (b)(3), and under (b)(4) the limits apply per individual debt, except that student loan debts serviced under a single account number when obtained by the collector count as one 'particular debt.'

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer gets 10 calls in 5 days from the in-house collections department of the bank that issued her credit card (or from a mortgage servicer collecting a loan it acquired before default). She asks whether the calls are unlawful under the 7-in-7 rule.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node never asks whether the caller is a 'debt collector' covered by the FDCPA/Regulation F. The 7-in-7 presumption in 12 CFR 1006.14(b)(2) applies only to covered debt collectors, not to original creditors collecting their own debts in their own name (and not to servicers of loans not in default at acquisition). As encoded, the rule would declare the calls presumptively unlawful under federal law when Reg F does not apply at all (any remedy would have to come from state law like the Rosenthal Act or TCPA).

edge_cases.scenario: Over one week a collector calls the consumer 4 times about a single medical debt and also calls the consumer's mother and her workplace 4 times about the same debt; the consumer adds them up and reports 8 calls in 7 days on one debt.
edge_cases.gap_description: The count under §1006.14(b)(2)(i) is per person AND per particular debt — calls to different people are not aggregated. The node encodes only the 'per particular debt' dimension, so it would find the 7-call threshold exceeded and declare a presumptive violation where none exists under the frequency rule (the third-party calls raise separate §1006.6(b)/§1006.10 issues the node does not address).

edge_cases.scenario: A Massachusetts consumer receives 5 calls in 7 days from a collection agency about one debt, with no conversation having occurred, and asks if the collector is doing anything wrong.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist never asks for the consumer's state. Several states impose stricter caps than the federal 7-in-7 safe harbor (e.g., Massachusetts 940 CMR 7.04 limits collectors to two telephone communications in a 7-day period; New York and other states have their own limits). As encoded, the node would report the calls as within the safe harbor / presumptively lawful, materially misleading a consumer who in fact has a state-law violation.

results.derivation_summary: Under 15 U.S.C. § 1692g(a), a debt collector must, in the initial communication or within five days after it (unless the debt is already paid), give the consumer written notice stating: the amount of the debt; the name of the creditor owed; that the debt will be assumed valid unless the consumer disputes it within thirty days of receiving the notice; that a written dispute within that thirty-day period triggers the collector's duty to obtain and mail verification of the debt or a copy of a judgment; and that on written request within the period the collector will supply the original creditor's name and address if different. Regulation F (12 C.F.R. § 1006.34(a)(1), (c)) permits the validation information to be given orally in the initial communication or by written notice in or within five days of it, and § 1006.34(b)(5) defines the 'validation period' as running from the date the information is provided until 30 days after the consumer receives or is assumed to receive it — the collector may assume receipt on any date at least five days (excluding legal public holidays, Saturdays, and Sundays) after providing it. Under § 1692g(b), a written dispute or request for the original creditor's name within the period requires the collector to cease collection of the disputed portion until verification, a judgment copy, or the creditor's name and address is mailed; otherwise, non-violative collection activity may continue during the 30-day period.

results.derivation_summary: Within five days after the initial collection communication, unless the information was already in that communication or the debt has been paid, the debt collector must send written notice stating the debt amount, the creditor’s name, and the consumer’s rights to dispute the debt, obtain verification or a judgment copy, and request the original creditor’s name and address if different. results.derivation_summary: A debt validation notice must contain specific information, including the amount of the debt, the name of the creditor, and several statements about the consumer's right to dispute the debt. The consumer has a 30-day window to dispute the debt, which starts when the consumer receives the validation information. For the purpose of calculating this 30-day period, the collector may assume the consumer received the notice five days after it was sent, excluding weekends and legal public holidays.

semantic_agreement_judge.agreement_notes: All three agree on the core rule: the validation notice (amount, creditor's name, dispute/verification rights) must be given in or within five days of the initial communication, the consumer has 30 days from receipt to dispute, and the collector may presume receipt five days after sending, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal public holidays. Completeness differences only: Analysis 1 adds the § 1692g(b) cease-collection-until-verification duty and the Regulation F option to provide validation information orally; Analysis 3 omits the five-day sending deadline and the itemized notice contents, and describes the period as starting at receipt rather than when information is provided — a phrasing nuance that does not change the practical end date.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer asks whether her dispute deadline has passed. The collector mailed the validation notice on a Friday; she wants to know the last day to dispute. The rule instructs: provided_date + 5 mailbox days + 30 days, 'computed per the exclusions above' (excluding Saturdays, Sundays, federal holidays).
edge_cases.gap_description: The encoded determination string applies the weekend/holiday exclusion ambiguously to the whole computation. Under 12 CFR 1006.34(b)(5) only the 5-day receipt assumption excludes Saturdays, Sundays, and legal public holidays; the 30-day validation period itself runs in calendar days. Applying the exclusion to the 30 days too pushes the end date roughly 10-12 days later, which can tell a consumer the window is still open when it closed, or cause a collector to state a wrong end date on the notice (itself a content violation). Deadline computation is the single most-used output of this node, so the ambiguity is material.

edge_cases.scenario: A collector mailed the validation notice to an address the consumer moved away from two years earlier; the mail was returned undeliverable and the consumer first learned of the debt from a credit report eight months later. She asks whether she can still dispute and force verification.
edge_cases.gap_description: The logic computes the window mechanically from the 'validation_info_provided_date' plus the 5-day receipt assumption, with no fact in the checklist for non-delivery, returned mail, or the collector's knowledge that the consumer did not receive the notice. Reg F's receipt assumption is a presumption tied to the validation period ending 30 days after the consumer 'receives or is assumed to receive' the information, and a collector with actual knowledge of non-receipt (returned mail) cannot rely on it; the notice may also fail 1692g entirely. As encoded, the node would tell a consumer with a live dispute right and a likely 1692g claim that her window closed months ago.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer is being called by the original creditor's own in-house collections department (or by a mortgage servicer that acquired the loan while current) and asks why she never received a validation notice and whether the 30-day dispute window applies.
edge_cases.gap_description: Neither the logic nor the completeness checklist contains any FDCPA coverage threshold: whether the entity is a 'debt collector' under 15 U.S.C. 1692a(6) (creditors collecting their own debts in their own name, and servicers who acquired the debt while not in default, are generally excluded) and whether the obligation is a consumer debt rather than a business/commercial one. Every checklist item is dispositive and none screens for this, so the node would generate a validation-notice analysis, a 30-day window, and a 'potential 1692g violation' flag for a person to whom 1692g does not apply at all. Original-creditor and servicer collection contacts are among the most common fact patterns consumers present.

results.derivation_summary: Under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a), an action on a contract, obligation, or liability founded on a written instrument must be brought within four years (with a special three-month limit for deficiency-type money judgments after a trustee's/mortgage power-of-sale). Section 337(d) provides that once that period has run, a person may not sue, arbitrate, or otherwise initiate legal proceedings to collect the debt, and the period may be extended only under Section 360. Section 360 allows extension only by a written acknowledgment or promise signed by the party charged, or by a payment of principal or interest (which restarts the clock from the date of payment), but expressly states no payment by itself revives a cause of action already barred. If the cause of action arose in another state or country and is time-barred there, § 361 bars suit in California as well (except for a California citizen who held the claim since it accrued); and once a money judgment is entered, § 683.020 makes it enforceable for 10 years from entry, renewable within that 10-year window.

Proc. § 337(a), an action on a contract, obligation, or liability founded on a written instrument must be brought within four years (with a special three-month limit for deficiency-type money judgments after a trustee's/mortgage power-of-sale). Section 337(d) provides that once that period has run, a person may not sue, arbitrate, or otherwise initiate legal proceedings to collect the debt, and the period may be extended only under Section 360. Section 360 allows extension only by a written acknowledgment or promise signed by the party charged, or by a payment of principal or interest (which restarts the clock from the date of payment), but expressly states no payment by itself revives a cause of action already barred. If the cause of action arose in another state or country and is time-barred there, § 361 bars suit in California as well (except for a California citizen who held the claim since it accrued); and once a money judgment is entered, § 683.020 makes it enforceable for 10 years from entry, renewable within that 10-year window.", "grounded": true, "citation_used": "Cal. Code Civ. Proc. \u00a7 337(a); see also \u00a7\u00a7 337(d), 360, 361, 683.020"}

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer defaulted on a credit card in 2019, filed Chapter 7 in 2022 and received a discharge, and in 2026 receives a collection letter and asks whether the debt is 'still good.' Under the encoded logic, accrual (2019) plus 4 years is less than today's date, so the node reports the claim time-barred; alternatively, if the default were 2023, it would report the claim live and collectible.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node has no bankruptcy dimension. A discharge permanently extinguishes personal liability regardless of the SOL, and the automatic stay plus 11 U.S.C. § 108(c)/CCP § 356 tolls the limitations period during the case. Neither the logic nor the checklist asks whether the debtor filed bankruptcy, so the node can (a) tell a discharged debtor the debt is merely 'expired' (understating a complete defense and missing a discharge-injunction violation claim) or (b) tell a debtor whose case tolled the clock that a claim is barred when it is not. Consumer bankruptcy is extremely common in exactly this fact pattern.

edge_cases.scenario: A borrower defaulted on a federal Direct/FFEL student loan in 2015, has made no payments, and asks in 2026 whether the government's servicer or a guaranty agency can still sue or garnish. The node classifies the promissory note as a signed written loan contract and applies the 4-year period.
edge_cases.gap_description: 20 U.S.C. § 1091a abolishes any statute of limitations for collection of federal student loans, and other categories the 'applies_to' language sweeps in (e.g., certain government-held obligations) are likewise not governed by CCP § 337. The node's applies_to/checklist never asks what type of obligation the written instrument evidences, so a defaulted federal student loan borrower would be told a decades-old debt is time-barred when it is permanently collectible — a materially wrong and potentially harmful conclusion.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer defaulted on a written retail installment contract in January 2020 (accelerated in full), and the creditor filed suit in California in May 2024. The consumer asks whether the suit was timely; the node compares the filing date to accrual-plus-four-years and reports the suit time-barred by about four months.
edge_cases.gap_description: California Judicial Council Emergency Rule 9(a) tolled all civil limitations periods over 180 days from April 6, 2020 to October 1, 2020 (178 days). That tolling applies automatically to every claim accruing before October 2020 — it is not a fact the consumer would 'suggest' in response to the checklist's generic tolling prompt. For the large cohort of pre-pandemic defaults litigated within a few months of the four-year line, the node's determination flips the bottom-line answer from timely to barred.
